results.result: Resting lymphocytes elongate at typical mammalian rates (~90-100s half-life), similar to HeLa cells and activated lymphocytes when measured by radiolabeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C46, C48, C51, and C52 collectively demonstrate that resting lymphocytes have ribosome transit times consistent with standard mammalian elongation rates (~6 residues/s). Multiple independent methods (RPM-RTA and [3H]-Leu incorporation) converge on similar half-life values (70-150s for HeLa, ~90-100s for lymphocytes), providing strong cross-validation of the measurements.

results.result: Lymphocyte elongation rates can be increased up to 30% by activation in vivo or fever temperature (39.5°C) in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C68, C73, C75, and C89 provide consistent evidence from multiple experimental conditions (in vivo activation, fever temperature in vitro) showing 20-30% increases in elongation rates. The measurements are internally consistent across different experimental systems (OT-I cells in vitro and in vivo), and the modified RTA protocol with CHX addresses methodological concerns about harringtonine leakiness (C156).

results.result: Resting and activated lymphocytes possess abundant monosome populations that contribute substantially to translation, with monosomes making major contributions in resting cells (~38% of translation) but minor contributions in fully activated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C53-C59, C104-C107, and C113-C114 provide converging evidence from polysome profiling, high-salt fractionation, puromycylation assays, and RTA measurements. The quantitative estimates (33-52% of monosomes puromycylated, ~38% of translation in resting cells) are based on direct measurements with appropriate controls. The distinction between in vitro stalling (C5, C60) and in vivo active translation (C4, C71, C72) is well-supported by differential RTA decay patterns.

results.result: A significant fraction of ex vivo cultured resting lymphocytes possess stalled ribosomes with nascent chains that are puromycylated but do not actively transit mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C49-C50, C60, and C96 demonstrate ribosome stalling through the key observation that RPM signal persists despite complete inhibition of [3H]-Leu incorporation (C40-C41) and limited RTA signal decay in emetine-treated cells. The interpretation is strengthened by comparison with neurons (C97) and the clear contrast with in vivo conditions where stalling is absent (C71-C72).

results.result: Nearly all ribosomes with nascent chains in both resting and activated lymphocytes are actively elongating in vivo, with no evidence of ribosome stalling in naive T cells in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by in vivo RTA experiments (C102) showing complete signal decay in both resting and activated cells, contrasting sharply with the in vitro stalling phenotype. The development and validation of the in vivo RTA method (C102, C151, C156-C158) provides technical support for these conclusions. The distinction between in vitro and in vivo translation states is a key finding.

results.result: In vivo activated OT-I T cells have a paradoxically high protein-to-ribosome ratio (1017:1) that dictates a minimal proteome duplication time of 22.2 hours, nearly 3× their measured doubling time of 7.7 hours, creating an unexplained discrepancy in protein synthesis capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C87-C88, C91 establish the core paradox through quantitative measurements of protein content, ribosome numbers, and division rates. The calculations are transparent and based on direct measurements (C119-C127). The discrepancy persists even when accounting for faster elongation rates in vivo (C89-C90, C160) and is exacerbated by protein degradation/secretion (C135-C138). Independent support comes from Wolf et al. 2020 (C140). However, the measurements rely on several assumptions (average protein length, tryptophan content) that could introduce systematic errors.

results.result: For HeLa cells and in vitro activated OT-I T cells, the calculated minimal proteome duplication time closely matches observed doubling times, indicating protein synthesis capacity is sufficient for cell division in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82, C132-C133 show that calculations based on measured protein and ribosome numbers yield proteome duplication times (19.9h for HeLa, 10.1h for OT-I) that are reasonably close to observed doubling times (24h and 9.7h respectively). This internal consistency validates the measurement and calculation approach, making the in vivo discrepancy (C6, C87-C88) more striking and less likely to be due to systematic measurement error.

results.result: The authors developed flow RPM-RTA, a simpler and cheaper method than existing approaches for measuring ribosome elongation rates at single-cell resolution, with improved accuracy through addition of elongation inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C92-C95 describe the methodological development and validation. The method is validated against established approaches (C46, C51) and shows improvement over the similar SunRiSE method (C94-C95) through addition of elongation inhibitors to reduce harringtonine leakiness. The single-cell capability (C93) and applicability to in vivo studies (C102-C103) represent significant technical advances.

results.result: OT-I T cells undergo substantial changes upon activation: ~2.9-fold volume increase, ~5-fold increase in protein content (from 421 million to 2.15 billion proteins/cell), 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration, and ~14-fold increase in ribosome numbers (from 264,000 to 3.6 million 60S subunits).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124, C127 provide quantitative characterization of T cell activation using multiple measurement approaches (automated cell counting, tryptophan fluorescence, bioanalyzer-based rRNA quantification). The measurements are internally consistent and the methods are well-described. The ribosome quantification method is noted as more accurate than prior approaches (C128). These measurements form the basis for the protein synthesis capacity calculations.

results.result: Activation induces a 15-fold increase in translating ribosomes in vivo (improved from 10-fold with better methods), but only a 2-5 fold increase by RPM in vitro, which is modest compared to historical 15-fold estimates from radiolabeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35, C99, C153 document the magnitude of activation-induced changes in protein synthesis. The improved in vivo RPM protocol (C151, C153) provides more accurate measurements than the original method. The discrepancy between RPM and radiolabeling (C34-C35) is explained by ribosome stalling in vitro (C42, C96), which affects RPM but not radiolabeling measurements.

results.result: An optimized activation protocol including SIINFEKL peptide with PHA and ionomycin is more effective than PMA/ionomycin alone, yielding large increases in polysome fractions and requiring 500mM salt (not 300mM) to fully dissociate non-translating ribosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111, C118 describe methodological improvements for T cell activation and polysome analysis. The superiority of the optimized protocol is demonstrated by multiple activation markers and functional readouts (C109). The salt concentration finding (C111) has implications for interpreting prior studies and for the monosome translation conclusions (C113-C114).

results.result: The authors speculate that lymphocytes may acquire proteins from other cells via mechanisms like emperipolesis or entosis to support their rapid division, though this remains unproven.
results.evaluation: Claims C141, C145, C147 present a speculative hypothesis to explain the protein synthesis paradox. While precedents exist for intercellular transfer of cellular components (C142-C144, C146), no direct evidence is provided for protein acquisition by lymphocytes. This is acknowledged as speculation (evidence_type: SPECULATION) and represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Human lymphocyte activation shows considerable donor heterogeneity in RPM staining and proliferation, with activated CD8+ T cells displaying a wide range of RPM staining and some divided cells returning to near-baseline RPM levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 document heterogeneity in human lymphocyte responses using CFSE dilution and RPM measurements. The observations are descriptive and well-supported by flow cytometry data, though the biological significance and mechanisms underlying this heterogeneity are not explored in depth.

results.result: Contrary to recent claims, puromycin does not completely release nascent chains from CHX-treated ribosomes; emetine is ineffective in vivo but cycloheximide is active in vivo for at least 60 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C151, C156 provide important methodological corrections and validations. The observation that puromycin does not completely release nascent chains (C149) contradicts recent publications and is supported by robust PMY signal in dot blots (Figure 5A). The in vivo activity of CHX (C151) enabled development of the improved in vivo RTA protocol (C156), which was critical for accurate in vivo elongation rate measurements.

results.result: The authors measured ribosome elongation rates in resting and activated lymphocytes using the RPM-RTA method, finding that resting lymphocytes elongate at typical mammalian rates (~6 residues/second, half-life 70-150s), similar to HeLa cells and activated lymphocytes. Elongation rates can be increased up to 30% by activation in vivo or fever temperature (39.5°C) in vitro.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted these findings. Reviewer 2 stated 'Elongation occurs at similar rates for HeLa cells and lymphocytes, with the active ribosomes in resting lymphocytes translating at a similar rate as fully activated lymphocytes.' The editor noted the work is 'supported by solid data.' No concerns were raised about the elongation rate measurements.

results.result: The authors found that resting and activated lymphocytes possess abundant monosome populations. In vitro, nearly all monosomes can be stalled prior to activation, while in vivo most monosomes actively translate. Approximately 33-52% of monosomes are puromycylated and contribute substantially to translation in resting cells (38%) but less in fully activated cells (32%).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly stated 'A large fraction of ribosomes are stalled in resting cultured primary human lymphocytes and these stalled ribosomes are likely to be monosomes.' The distinction between in vitro stalling and in vivo active translation was noted by Reviewer 2 who commented on the 'Day1 resting T-cells also show stalling - which curiously wasn't seen on freshly purified cells' but did not dispute the findings.

results.result: The authors quantified protein mass, ribosome numbers, and division rates to calculate that activated lymphocytes have a paradoxically high protein-to-ribosome ratio insufficient to support their rapid in vivo division. For in vivo activated OT-I cells, the minimal proteome duplication time (22.2 hours) is nearly 3× the measured doubling time (7.7 hours), suggesting the activated lymphocyte proteome may be generated in an unusual manner.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant concerns about this central conclusion. Reviewer 1 stated the primary conclusion 'remains, to my eye, insufficiently supported by the data' and noted 'the devil is deeper in the details' requiring additional molecular accounting including mRNA transcriptome composition, protein half-life changes, and other parameters. Reviewer 1 proposed an alternative interpretation where 'the quiescent state is biologically poised to support activation' with surplus inventory. While reviewers found the paradox interesting and provocative, they did not fully accept the conclusion without additional evidence.

results.result: The authors developed flow RTA, a method to measure translation elongation rates that is simpler and cheaper than existing methods, provides single-cell information, and can be used in vivo by intravenous delivery of translation inhibitors. The addition of elongation inhibitors (CHX or EME) to the protocol reduces harringtonine leakiness and improves accuracy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the methodological advances without challenge. Reviewer 2 noted 'Lots of interesting techniques' and the editor stated the work is 'supported by solid data.' Reviewer 1 acknowledged 'the use of orthogonal approaches to validate the primary findings' as a strength. No concerns were raised about the RTA methodology itself.

results.result: Using the improved RPM protocol, the authors measured a ~15-fold increase in translating ribosomes in activated OT-I T cells in vivo compared to resting cells. This is more modest than the ~15-fold increase reported in original studies using radiolabeling, but represents an improvement over their previously reported 10-fold increase.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these quantitative measurements. The methodological improvements were implicitly accepted as the reviewers focused their concerns on the interpretation and implications of the measurements rather than the measurements themselves.

results.result: The authors found that an optimized activation protocol including SIINFEKL antigenic stimulation with PHA and ionomycin is more effective than PMA/ionomycin alone, yielding large increases in polysome fractions and greatly increasing the fraction of ribosomes in polysomes on day 1 post-activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this methodological finding. Reviewer 3 suggested the human T cell data should be omitted or downplayed because 'the activation status achieved was less than that seen for the OT-1 model,' implicitly accepting the superiority of the optimized protocol for mouse cells.

results.result: The authors quantified cellular parameters during T cell activation: OT-I T cells increase in diameter with a ~2.9-fold volume increase, protein content increases ~5-fold (from 421 million to 2.15 billion proteins per cell), resulting in a 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration. The 60S subunit increases from 264,000 to ~3.6 million copies per cell, and the protein-to-ribosome ratio drops up to 3-fold during activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these quantitative measurements. Reviewer 1 noted the study includes 'quantitative, biochemical determinations of protein and ribosome content' as a strength. The measurements themselves were accepted; concerns focused on their interpretation and what additional parameters might be needed.

results.result: The authors propose that lymphocytes may resort to acquiring proteins from resting lymphocytes or other cell types (perhaps via emperipolesis or entosis) to support their rapid division, and conclude that much remains to be learned about basic lymphocyte cell biology and the importance of simple accounting.
results.evaluation: Reviewers treated this as highly speculative. Reviewer 1 noted the authors 'hint at cellular mechanisms to explain this apparent paradox' but stated 'several cellular regulatory processes that could explain the apparent paradox are not explored.' The editor noted the study 'proposes non-conventional mechanisms' and 'sets the scene for further work,' indicating acceptance of the speculation as hypothesis-generating rather than established fact.

results.result: The authors observed considerable donor heterogeneity in RPM staining and proliferation of human lymphocyte subpopulations, with activated CD8+ T cells showing a wide range of RPM staining on day 2, and approximately 50% of non-activated cells demonstrating increased RPM staining despite not dividing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these observations about human lymphocytes, though Reviewer 3 suggested omitting the human data altogether because of inferior activation compared to the OT-1 model. The observations themselves were not disputed.

results.result: The authors found that elongation inhibitors had minor effects on RPM of activated or resting cells, while initiation inhibitors clearly discriminated between resting and activated cells, diminishing RPM signal by 80-90% on day 5 post-activation. All inhibitors nearly completely blocked [3H]-Leu incorporation, suggesting actively translating ribosomes in resting cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these experimental observations with translation inhibitors. The findings were used to support the interpretation of stalled ribosomes, which reviewers accepted for in vitro conditions.

results.result: The authors confirmed that resting lymphocytes have few polysomes with a large fraction of ribosomes fractionating as monosomes in sucrose gradients. Polysome abundance increases over 2 days post-activation. High salt (500 mM) was necessary to fully dissociate non-translating ribosomes, and monosomes in resting lymphocytes are stable in high salt, indicating active translation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these polysome profiling findings without challenge. The observations confirmed prior literature and were used to support the monosome translation conclusions.

results.result: The authors found that nearly all ribosomes with nascent chains in both resting and activated lymphocytes are actively elongating proteins in vivo, and contrary to in vitro observations, ribosomes are not stalled in naive mouse T cells in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this key distinction between in vitro and in vivo conditions. Reviewer 2 noted the finding and commented on the curiosity of the difference but did not dispute it. The in vivo RTA data supporting this conclusion were not challenged.

results.result: The authors note that Wolf et al., 2020 mass spectrometric-based measurements of in vitro T cell protein synthetic capacity support and even exacerbate the paradox.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 extensively discussed the Wolf et al. study, noting 'Many other elements of the Wolf paper seem quite relevant' and suggesting additional accounting based on that work. The reviewer did not dispute that Wolf et al. data support the paradox, but argued more detailed analysis is needed.

results.result: The authors found that emetine was ineffective in vivo for stabilizing puromycylated polypeptides on ribosomes, but cycloheximide is active in vivo, arresting accumulation of puromycylated polypeptides for at least 60 minutes. Addition of CHX to in vivo RTA is important because of harringtonine's leakiness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these methodological findings about inhibitor effectiveness in vivo. The improvements to the RTA protocol were implicitly accepted.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the findings on elongation rates in resting lymphocytes (C1, C46, C48, C51, C52). OpenEval emphasizes convergence of multiple methods and cross-validation. Peer reviewers explicitly accepted these findings with Reviewer 2 stating elongation occurs at similar rates for HeLa cells and lymphocytes. Complete agreement.

OpenEval R2 addresses activation-induced increases in elongation rates (C2, C68, C73, C89) with 20-30% increases. Peer R1 partially overlaps (C68, C73, C89) and accepts similar elongation rates between resting and activated lymphocytes. Both support the findings though OpenEval emphasizes the increase while peer review notes similarity.

Both evaluations address monosome translation and ribosome stalling (C3, C4, C5, C104-C107, C113-C114). OpenEval finds converging evidence from multiple assays supporting active monosome translation. Peer reviewers explicitly accepted these findings with Reviewer 2 stating 'A large fraction of ribosomes are stalled in resting cultured primary human lymphocytes and these stalled ribosomes are likely to be monosomes.' Complete agreement.

OpenEval R4 addresses in vitro ribosome stalling (C42, C49, C50, C60, C96). Peer R2 includes these claims and accepts the stalling findings. Both evaluations support the conclusion that ribosomes stall in vitro culture conditions. Complete agreement on the stalling phenomenon.

Both evaluations address the distinction between in vitro stalling and in vivo active translation (C71, C72). OpenEval emphasizes the complete RTA signal decay in vivo contrasting with in vitro stalling. Peer reviewers accepted this key distinction, with Reviewer 2 noting the finding without disputing it. Complete agreement.

Both evaluations address the central protein synthesis paradox (C6, C7, C83-C88, C90-C91, C135, C138, C160). OpenEval finds the paradox well-supported by quantitative measurements despite acknowledging assumptions. Peer reviewers expressed significant concerns, with Reviewer 1 stating the conclusion 'remains, to my eye, insufficiently supported' and proposing alternative interpretations. Major disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

OpenEval R7 addresses internal consistency of proteome duplication calculations (C79-C82, C132-C133) as validation. Peer R3 includes some overlapping claims (C79, C81, C82) but focuses on the broader paradox. OpenEval views these calculations as supporting evidence; peer reviewers question whether additional molecular accounting is needed. Partial disagreement on interpretation.

Both evaluations address RTA methodological development and validation (C92-C95, C102-C103). OpenEval emphasizes technical advances including single-cell capability and in vivo applicability. Peer reviewers accepted the methodology without challenge, with Reviewer 2 noting 'Lots of interesting techniques.' Complete agreement on methodological validity.

Both evaluations address quantitative characterization of T cell activation (C119-C124, C127). OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency and improved accuracy of ribosome quantification. Peer reviewers accepted these measurements, with Reviewer 1 noting 'quantitative, biochemical determinations' as a strength. Complete agreement on measurement validity.

Both evaluations address activation-induced changes in protein synthesis (C34, C35, C99, C153). OpenEval emphasizes improved in vivo RPM protocol and explains RPM-radiolabeling discrepancy. Peer reviewers accepted the quantitative measurements without challenge. Complete agreement.

Both evaluations address methodological improvements for T cell activation (C109, C110, C118). OpenEval emphasizes superiority demonstrated by multiple markers. Peer reviewers accepted the finding, with Reviewer 3 implicitly accepting the optimized protocol's superiority for mouse cells. Complete agreement.

Both evaluations address the speculative hypothesis of intercellular protein transfer (C141, C145, C147). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging it as speculation for future testing. Peer reviewers treated it as highly speculative, with the editor noting it 'sets the scene for further work.' Complete agreement that this is hypothesis-generating rather than established fact.

Both evaluations address heterogeneity in human lymphocyte responses (C28-C33). OpenEval finds observations well-supported but notes limited exploration of mechanisms. Peer reviewers did not challenge the observations, though Reviewer 3 suggested omitting human data due to inferior activation. Agreement on observations, with peer review questioning emphasis.

Both evaluations address methodological corrections regarding puromycin and in vivo CHX activity (C150, C151, C156). OpenEval emphasizes importance for accurate in vivo measurements and contradiction of recent publications. Peer reviewers accepted these methodological findings without challenge. Complete agreement.

OpenEval R3 includes polysome profiling findings (C53, C54, C56-C58) as part of broader evidence for monosome translation. Peer R11 addresses these same polysome profiling claims and accepts them as confirming prior literature. Complete agreement on these specific findings.

Both evaluations address translation inhibitor experiments (C37, C38 overlap, with peer R10 also including C36, C40, C41). OpenEval emphasizes these support the stalling interpretation. Peer reviewers accepted the experimental observations and their use in supporting stalled ribosome interpretation. Complete agreement.

OpenEval R5 addresses in vivo RTA method development (C102, C103) as part of demonstrating no in vivo stalling. Peer R4 accepts the methodological advances including in vivo applicability. Complete agreement on methodological validity.

Peer R13 addresses support from Wolf et al. 2020 study (C140) for the protein synthesis paradox. OpenEval mentions C140 in R6 as independent support but does not have a dedicated result. Peer Reviewer 1 extensively discussed Wolf et al. and suggested additional accounting based on that work.
